why: If every segment has even length, every segment boundary falls at an even index, so the string is really a sequence of pairs. A mixed pair ('01'/'10') costs exactly one flip and can take either colour; a pure pair costs nothing and fixes a colour. The minimum flips is the number of mixed pairs, and greedily giving each mixed pair a neighbour's colour leaves segments = colour changes among pure pairs + 1.
hints: Every segment has even length, so where can boundaries be? Try cutting the string into consecutive pairs.

Each pair must end up uniform. A mixed pair needs exactly 1 flip; a pure pair needs 0 (flipping it to the other colour costs 2, which is never minimal). So B = number of mixed pairs, and pure pairs keep their colour.

Mixed pairs can join whichever neighbour they like, so skip them. Walk the pure pairs and count how many times their colour changes; segments = changes + 1, or 1 if there are no pure pairs. One pass: O(n).
pitfalls: Minimise flips first: do not recolour a pure pair just to merge segments.
If every pair is mixed, the answer is 1 (make them all the same colour).
A flip changes a single character, not a whole frame range.
statement:
A video has n frames (n is even), given as a binary string frames. In one flip you change a single character: 0 becomes 1 or 1 becomes 0.

After flipping, the string must be split into contiguous subsegments such that:

  • each subsegment contains only one character (all 0s or all 1s), and
  • each subsegment has even length.

First use the minimum possible number of flips B. Among all ways that use exactly B flips, return the minimum number of subsegments.

Example: frames = "1110011000".

  1. Even-length segments mean every boundary sits at an even index, so look at pairs: 11 | 10 | 01 | 10 | 00.
  2. The three mixed pairs each need one flip, so B = 3. The pure pairs 11 and 00 need none.
  3. Turn every mixed pair into 11: "1111111100".
  4. This splits into 11111111 and 00, both even, so 2 subsegments.

The answer is 2.
